newsitem.title: USA: SEC probe of "yield burning" positive sign-lawyers.
newsitem.headline: SEC probe of "yield burning" positive sign-lawyers.

text.p: Bond lawyers said on Monday that Prudential Securities Inc's disclosure of an SEC subpoena concerning possible "yield burning" in a Pennsylvania debt offering is good news for municipal bond issuers.
Yield burning refers to allegations that bond underwriters overcharge issuers for U.S. Treasury securities purchased in the open market and used in bond refinancing transactions.

Reuters reported last week that Prudential received a Securities and Exchange Commission subpoena in May 1996 concerning escrow securities that it sold Pennsylvania for a 1993 certificates of participation deal.

The firm disclosed the information in a response to a November 1996 Orange County, Fla., School Board request for proposals from senior underwriters for an upcoming bond offering. Florida's policy is to make responses to bond RFPs public.

Bond lawyers said SEC's involvement is good news because the SEC can use the federal securities laws to take action against dealers that sold so-called escrow bonds to unwitting state and local governments.
Lawyers want the Internal Revenue Service to withdraw a controversial July 1996 notice that tells localities if they pay certain penalities they can avoid having their bonds declared taxable.
"This is properly the jurisdiction of the SEC," former Treasury Department official David Walton told Reuters.
"The IRS should leave innocent issuers that acted with due diligence alone," said Walton, a partner with Jones Hall Hill & White in San Francisco.

Amy Dunbar, government affairs director for the National Association of Bond Lawyers, said, "SEC oversees and regulates pricing practices. They are the (ones) who can enforce against the people who violated the laws."
By using the tax laws, "you can only go after the issuer who is a victim rather than perpetrator," she said.

The SEC's Pennsylvania probe is an outgrowth of a broad federal investigation of yield burning launched in fall 1995. The SEC sent subpoenas to 20 of the top municipal bond underwriters in the country seeking information about 25 big advance refunding deals done in 1991, 1992 and 1993.
Other bond firms responding to the Orange County, Fla., RFP said they have received inquiries concerning yield burning from the SEC.

Smith Barney said, "The SEC is conducting one or more wideranging investigations into various practices in the municipal finance business generally, including reinvestment and escrow pricing ("yield burning") and the process by which underwriters are selected."

"These investigations have included subpoenas and requests for information from the SEC to a number of issuers and participants in many different transactions, including some in which Smith Barney participated as underwriter or otherwise," the firm said.
And other firms said they had been contacted by federal probers about municipal bond deals, but the firms did not say whether the investigations involved yield burning.

PaineWebber Inc said in its response that, "Recently, the SEC has undertaken a broad-based investigation of the municipal securities industry and, in connection therewith, PaineWebber and other large firms have been asked to provide information. PaineWebber is fully cooperating."
